drapeaux.note: Minister Christine Albanel's words “pour la troisième fois depuis sa découverte” were spoken in French (answer to oral question no. 157, Assemblée nationale, 2008; French wording seen in the record: https://www.assemblee-nationale.fr/dyn/13/questions/QANR5L13QOSD157.pdf). No published English translation exists; official English text not retrieved, so the rendering “for the third time since its discovery” is a faithful translation.

titre: Lascaux Was Closed to the Public, and the Mold Came Anyway
accroche: In 1963, green algae and calcite force Lascaux to close to the public. In 2001, after work on the cave's air system, a fungus invades it.
contenu_vulgarise:
Lascaux is the cave that was closed to protect it from its visitors. The story is accurate, but it stops too soon.

In September 1962, according to the researchers who have traced the cave's biological management, a first spot of green algae appears on the walls, after twelve years of uninterrupted visits that brought an excess of carbon dioxide and light. The “green sickness” is added to a “white sickness,” a veil of calcite. The Minister of Culture André Malraux decides to close the cave to the public on April 18, 1963. A formaldehyde solution diluted to 1/200 is applied to the rock, the floors, and the paintings, and within four months the cave is rid of green algae.

## A Closed Cave, Not a Frozen One

The same researchers mention a limit of at most five visitors a day, under diffuse lighting. According to them, no visible manifestation appears until 1994, and a preventive treatment continues until 1998.

In September 2001, however, a white down of mycelium covers the floors, the ledges, and part of the sloping surfaces within a few days. The fungus is identified as Fusarium solani, associated, according to the Minister of Culture in 2008, with a bacterium abundant in the surrounding agricultural soils. The invasion occurs after a round of work on the cave's air management system. For the authors of the chapter, the most plausible hypothesis is that Fusarium, dominant throughout the cavity, took advantage of conditions favorable to germination when the air-handling units were being overhauled: the microclimate changes would have triggered the simultaneous germination of several strains. They also cite, among the possible routes of introduction, percolation water and the input of outside soil by visitors, small animals, or runoff. A first treatment with quaternary ammonium proves ineffective; quicklime is spread on the floors at the end of October 2001.

## More Than One Danger

In 2008, before the National Assembly, Minister Christine Albanel declares that the cave is a victim of a bioclimatic disruption that favors the proliferation of microorganisms, “for the third time since its discovery.” After the green algae and then the white mold of 2001 came black spots, due mostly to a fungus of the genus Ulocladium.

Removing the public did not freeze the cave in place. The balance among rock, air, and microorganisms remained to be maintained, and the 2001 invasion occurs after an intervention on the air, not after visitors returned. The public, for its part, has been visiting a facsimile, Lascaux II, since 1983. What, in a cave with restricted access, maintains that balance remains to be established.

repere.texte: The first spot of green algae appears in September 1962, after twelve years of uninterrupted visits; the cave is closed to the public in 1963.
repere.source: Orial, Bousta, François, Pallot-Frossard, and Warscheid, “Gestion des activités biologiques à Lascaux (Management of Biological Activities at Lascaux),” chap. 9 of Lascaux et la conservation en milieu souterrain (Lascaux and Conservation in Underground Settings), Éditions de la MSH, pp. 219-251, § 9.3.2

carte.punch: Closed to the public in 1963, Lascaux suffered a mold invasion in 2001.
carte.idee: Visitors brought carbon dioxide and light, and green algae led to Lascaux's closure to the public in 1963. But the cave remained exposed: after work on the air management system, a fungus, Fusarium solani, invaded the cave in September 2001.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: In English. Same chapter, with details of the treatments and the 2007 episode.

quiz.question: What does the mold episode of September 2001 at Lascaux show, nearly forty years after the closure of 1963?
choix: That reopening the cave to the public in 2001 brought back the fungus that visitors before 1963 had left there
That a closed cave remains exposed: a fungus invaded it after work on the air management system
That the 1963 closure had been pointless, since the green algae came back in the same proportions
That the scientists admitted to the cave after 1963 brought the fungus in, so its return has nothing to do with the air
quiz.explication: The cave had been closed to the public for nearly forty years when Fusarium solani invaded it, shortly after work on its air management system: the public, for its part, was visiting a facsimile. For the authors of the chapter, the most plausible hypothesis is that Fusarium already dominant in the cavity germinated thanks to microclimate changes; they also cite soil brought in by visitors among the possible routes of introduction, without making it the established cause. The green algae, for their part, had disappeared within four months after treatment and did not return.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What caused the closure of Lascaux to the public in 1963?
choix: An invasion of white mold identified as Fusarium solani
The appearance of green algae and a veil of calcite after twelve years of uninterrupted visits
Work on the cave's air management system judged too costly
The discovery of black spots caused by a fungus of the genus Ulocladium
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The “green sickness” and the “white sickness” appear in 1962 after twelve years of visits, leading to the closure of 1963. Fusarium solani and the Ulocladium spots are episodes much later.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What preceded the Fusarium solani invasion of September 2001?
choix: A temporary reopening of the cave to a group of scientific visitors
A raising of the daily visitor limit, from five to twenty people
A round of work on the cave's air management system
The disappearance of the veil of calcite detected in 1963, then judged definitive
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 2001 invasion occurs after a round of work on the cave's air management system; nothing in the text mentions a reopening to the public or a raising of the visitor limit.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is the hypothesis the authors of the chapter consider most plausible to explain the 2001 invasion?
choix: Fusarium fungi already present in the cave germinated thanks to the microclimate changes linked to the work
Spores brought in by the filming of a documentary in 2001 contaminated the floors
The 1963 formaldehyde treatment weakened the rock and favored fungi
A rainwater leak introduced the fungus from outside in a single night
quiz_supplementaire.explication: For the authors, the most plausible hypothesis is that Fusarium already dominant in the cavity germinated thanks to the microclimate changes caused by the overhaul of the air-handling units, not a film shoot or a leak.
